title: How LLD Is Evaluated in Interviews

content.title: How LLD Is Evaluated in Interviews

blocks.content: Interviewers don't have a fixed checklist but they all look for the same underlying signals. Understanding exactly what gets you hired vs. what gets you rejected makes preparation specific instead of vague.
THE OVERALL EVALUATION SCORECARD
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/6644b336-4010-451c-bd5b-5178f6f65947.png
1. The 6 criteria
1. Class design quality
Weight: very high, this is the foundation of everything
Every class should have one clear job. Every attribute should belong to that class and nowhere else.
Methods should be named so clearly that reading the signature tells you exactly what it does. Interviewers read class names and immediately know if you understand responsibility.
GOOD DESIGN VS BAD DESIGN: SAME SYSTEM
blocks.text: GOOD DESIGN VS BAD DESIGN: SAME SYSTEM

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/e42ca626-2494-4c06-8471-17e560f0ae06.png
RED FLAGS
God classes with 10+ methods, attributes that don't belong, vague method names like process() or handle()
GREEN FLAGS
Small focused classes, expressive names like calculateDeliveryFee(), private fields with public methods
2. OOP depth
Weight: high, every decision should show OOP instinct
Knowing what encapsulation means is not enough. Interviewers want to see you use it making fields private, exposing only what's needed, using abstractions instead of concrete types.
Most candidates can define the four pillars. Few apply them naturally under pressure.
WHAT EACH PILLAR LOOKS LIKE IN AN INTERVIEW ANSWER

WHAT SEPARATES GOOD FROM GREAT: Good candidates name the pillars. Great candidates say "I'm making PaymentProcessor an interface, not an abstract class, because callers should depend on the contract not the implementation that's abstraction working with dependency inversion."
3. Design pattern recognition
Weight: high, shows you've solved problems before

Patterns show pattern. When you naturally reach for an Observer to handle notifications, or a Strategy to swap pricing algorithms, interviewers see someone who has thought through these problems before not someone improvising from scratch.
The key is: never name-drop a pattern just to sound smart. Always tie it to the specific problem it solves in your design.
PATTERN → PROBLEM IT SOLVES
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/48aa9c98-6a2e-4717-a462-a7cac5132c3d.png
RED FLAG
"I'll use a Factory here": with no explanation of why or what problem it solves.
GREEN FLAG
"I'll use a Factory so the caller never needs to know which NotificationSender gets created that's the creation logic's job."
4. Extensibility: can the design handle change?
blocks.text: 4. Extensibility: can the design handle change?

blocks.content: Weight: high, real systems always change
After you present your design, every interviewer asks some version of: "What if we now need to add X?" They want to see whether you hardcoded assumptions into the design or left it open to change.
A design that requires editing 5 existing classes to add one new payment method has failed this criterion even if it works today.
When the system is poorly designed, adding a new feature requires changing existing code in many places. This increases complexity and can introduce bugs.
A better design allows new features to be added by creating new classes or modules without changing old working code.
This is called the Open/Closed Principle:
["Open for extension","Closed for modification"]
5. Trade-off articulation
Weight: medium-high, separates engineers from architects
No design is perfect. The best engineers know this and they say it out loud. When you make a choice, name the alternative you didn't pick and explain why this one fits the current constraints better.
WEAK ANSWER
"I used inheritance here because it works."
STRONG ANSWER
"I chose composition over inheritance here inheritance would couple the lifecycle too tightly and make testing harder when we mock dependencies."
THE MAGIC PHRASE
"The trade-off here is…" saying this triggers the interviewer's mental green flag. It signals you understand there is no free lunch in software design.
6. Communication: thinking out loud
Weight: high, in design, silence is a red flag
LLD is a collaborative round, not a solo exam. Interviewers can't evaluate what's inside your head only what you say.
Candidates who narrate their reasoning, ask clarifying questions before diving in, and explain decisions as they make them score significantly higher than equally-skilled but quiet candidates.
WHAT A STRONG CANDIDATE SOUNDS LIKE
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-content-images/e11c0508-e914-4be5-84cc-73b3107d50ce.png
The instant hire vs instant reject signals
INSTANT HIRE SIGNALS

• Names and applies a pattern correctly without prompting
• Says "the trade-off here is…" naturally
• Spots that requirements changed and adjusts the design
• Asks "should this be an interface or abstract class?" and answers it themselves
• Design survives the "what if we add X?" follow-up
INSTANT REJECT SIGNALS

• One class that does everything
• Can't explain why they chose one relationship type over another
• Goes silent for 10+ minutes
• Applies a pattern they can't explain when asked
• Design breaks when one requirement changes
THE MOST UNDERRATED CRITERION
Iteration. Candidates who say "actually, let me reconsider this if X changes, my current design breaks, so let me restructure this part" score higher than those who defend a flawed first attempt.
Interviewers hire for how you think, not whether your first answer is perfect.
2. Three more criteria that quietly decide the outcome
blocks.text: 2. Three more criteria that quietly decide the outcome

blocks.content: The six criteria above cover the design itself. The three below cover everything that happens around the design, before you draw a class and after the happy path works, and interviewers weigh them just as heavily even though candidates rarely study for them directly.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783512577967-148607864.png
blocks.alt: Timeline of a typical LLD interview round moving from clarifying scope through designing core classes, the happy path, what if follow ups, and finally naming trade offs explicitly

blocks.content: 7. Requirement clarification: the scorecard starts before the whiteboard
blocks.text: 7. Requirement clarification: the scorecard starts before the whiteboard

blocks.content: Weight: high, most early rejections trace back here

Interviewers watch the first two or three minutes closer than almost anything else that follows. A candidate who starts sketching classes before knowing whether the system needs one warehouse or a thousand is optimizing for the wrong problem, and every decision after that opening gets built on a guess instead of a stated assumption. The bar isn't a long interrogation, it's two or three sharp questions: who are the actors, what is the core flow the interviewer actually cares about, and what can safely be pushed out of scope for this session.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783512580712-879806663.png
blocks.alt: Decision flow a candidate should follow before drawing any class, asking who the actors are, what the core flow is, and what is out of scope, then restating agreed scope before beginning class design

blocks.content: WEAK OPENING VS STRONG OPENING

WEAK: "Okay, let me start designing classes for a parking lot system," no scope, no actors, no constraints stated, just code.

STRONG: "Before I design anything, quick clarification, are we supporting multiple vehicle types and multiple entry points, and is payment part of this session or can I stub it out?"

RED FLAG: diving straight into class names within the first thirty seconds, it signals the candidate treats LLD as a coding exercise rather than a design conversation.

GREEN FLAG: two or three targeted questions, then a one line summary of the agreed scope before writing anything, "So to confirm, I will design for a single lot, multiple vehicle types, no payment for now."
8. Code quality and naming: the quiet scorer running the whole time
blocks.text: 8. Code quality and naming: the quiet scorer running the whole time

blocks.content: Weight: medium to high, compounds silently across the round

Every method signature and variable name written on the shared doc is being read in real time. Interviewers rarely stop to comment on naming mid round, they just quietly note it, and a pile of small naming misses reads as sloppiness even when the underlying design is sound. Magic numbers, one letter variables, and methods named after implementation details instead of intent are the most common ways strong design gets undermined by weak code quality.
SAME METHOD, TWO NAMING STYLES

RED FLAG: parameters named a, b, x, temp, magic numbers like status equal to 1 instead of a named constant or enum.

GREEN FLAG: constants and enums for anything that isn't self evident, method names that read like a sentence describing what they return.
9. Edge case handling: the differentiator most candidates skip
blocks.text: 9. Edge case handling: the differentiator most candidates skip

blocks.content: Weight: medium, separates a design that compiles from one that survives production

Most candidates design the happy path and stop. The last few minutes of a strong round are usually spent on the interviewer asking what happens if, and watching whether the design already accounts for it or needs to be patched on the spot. The specific edge cases vary by problem, but the categories repeat across almost every LLD prompt.

["Concurrent access, two threads booking the same seat or slot at the same time","Invalid or missing input, a null customer, a negative quantity, an unknown enum value","Capacity limits, what happens when the parking lot, cache, or queue is already full","Partial failure, payment succeeds but notification fails, does the whole operation roll back"]
items: Concurrent access, two threads booking the same seat or slot at the same time
Invalid or missing input, a null customer, a negative quantity, an unknown enum value
Capacity limits, what happens when the parking lot, cache, or queue is already full
Partial failure, payment succeeds but notification fails, does the whole operation roll back

blocks.content:
RED FLAG: only discovering these cases when the interviewer asks, and needing to redesign core classes to handle them because nothing was left open for it.

GREEN FLAG: naming at least one edge case unprompted while designing, even briefly, "I'll assume single threaded for now, but if we needed concurrency safety here I'd add a lock or a compare and swap on the slot state."
3. The complete rubric and how to avoid the classic mistakes
blocks.text: 3. The complete rubric and how to avoid the classic mistakes

blocks.content: Put together, the nine dimensions above form the rubric most interviewers are running in their head, even if they never write it down. Seeing them side by side makes it obvious where actual prep time should go, and it's rarely more pattern trivia.

{"headers":["Dimension","Weight","What a strong answer sounds like"],"rows":[["Class design quality","Very high","Small focused classes, expressive method names, one clear job each"],["OOP depth","High","Names the pillar and the reason, not just the definition"],["Design pattern recognition","High","Ties every pattern to the specific problem it solves"],["Extensibility","High","New feature needs a new class, not edits across five old ones"],["Trade-off articulation","Medium to high","States the alternative not picked, and why"],["Communication","High","Narrates reasoning continuously, asks before assuming"],["Requirement clarification","High","Two or three sharp questions before any class is drawn"],["Code quality and naming","Medium to high","Self documenting names, constants instead of magic numbers"],["Edge case handling","Medium","Names at least one edge case unprompted"]]}
RED FLAGS THAT SINK AN OTHERWISE STRONG CANDIDATE
blocks.text: RED FLAGS THAT SINK AN OTHERWISE STRONG CANDIDATE

blocks.content: None of these are about knowing less design, they are about how the knowledge gets applied under time pressure.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783512582453-160766116.png
blocks.alt: Red flag versus green flag branch when an interviewer asks what if we add a new feature, redesigning existing classes reads as fragile while adding one new class reads as extensible

blocks.content: ["Jumping straight into class names before scope is agreed on","Reaching for three patterns when the problem needed one, just to look impressive","Parameter and method names that hide intent instead of revealing it","A design that only survives the happy path and breaks on the first what if","Going quiet for long stretches instead of narrating trade-offs as they are made"]
items: Jumping straight into class names before scope is agreed on
Reaching for three patterns when the problem needed one, just to look impressive
Parameter and method names that hide intent instead of revealing it
A design that only survives the happy path and breaks on the first what if
Going quiet for long stretches instead of narrating trade-offs as they are made

blocks.content: NARRATING YOUR THINKING LIKE A STRONG CANDIDATE
blocks.text: NARRATING YOUR THINKING LIKE A STRONG CANDIDATE

blocks.content: This is roughly what a strong candidate sounds like out loud during the first few minutes of a parking lot problem, notice how little of it is actual code.

blocks.title: WHAT A STRONG CANDIDATE SOUNDS LIKE OUT LOUD
blocks.text: So we have a parking lot, multiple floors, multiple vehicle types, entry and exit gates. Let me start with the actors, Vehicle, ParkingSpot, Ticket, and the lot itself as a coordinator, ParkingLot. I'll make ParkingSpot an interface since a compact spot and a bike spot behave differently, callers shouldn't depend on one concrete shape. For assigning spots, I could hardcode the search logic, but if we ever need a different assignment policy, nearest first versus cheapest first, that's a Strategy, so I'll pull it into a SpotAssignmentStrategy interface now rather than retrofit it later. The trade-off here is a bit more upfront structure for flexibility we may not use, but parking assignment logic tends to change often enough in real systems that I think it's worth it.

blocks.content: That one paragraph already touches class design, an interface decision, a named pattern tied to a real reason, and an explicit trade-off. None of it required extra time, it just required narrating the decision instead of making it silently.
